prompt: Write the introduction section of an academic paper titled “Self-identity in anorexia nervosa”. The paper is in philosophy of psychiatry. About 700 words. Output only the text of the introduction, with no heading.
raw:
Among psychiatric conditions, anorexia nervosa is unusual in how often those who have it describe the illness as part of who they are. Patients frequently report that the disorder feels less like something that has happened to them than like an expression of their character, values, and will. Some speak of anorexia as a companion, a source of strength, or a protective presence. Others say that without it they would not know who they were. In qualitative studies, the language of identity recurs. Participants describe anorexia as having become "part of me," and they express fear that recovery would mean losing themselves (Tan, Hope, and Stewart 2003). Clinicians have long noted this feature, and they often characterise the disorder as "ego-syntonic." Its central beliefs and desires, above all the commitment to thinness and the pursuit of control over eating, are experienced as consonant with the self rather than as intrusions upon it.

This phenomenology creates difficulties that are at once clinical, ethical, and philosophical. Clinically, it helps explain why anorexia is notoriously resistant to treatment and why ambivalence about recovery is the norm. Ethically, it complicates the assessment of decision-making capacity. A person with severe anorexia may understand, retain, and reason about information concerning her condition. She may nonetheless refuse life-sustaining nutrition on the basis of values that she endorses, yet which seem to have been shaped, perhaps wholly constituted, by the disorder itself. Standard cognitive tests of capacity struggle to register what has gone wrong in such cases, if anything has. This has led some theorists to argue that the relevant impairment concerns not reasoning but values (Tan et al. 2006). Others have turned to the concept of authenticity, asking whether choices made under the influence of anorexia genuinely belong to the person who makes them (Hope et al. 2011).

Underlying these debates is a question that philosophy of psychiatry has not yet adequately answered: what is the relationship between anorexia nervosa and the self of the person who has it? Two broad answers are commonly assumed, often implicitly. The first, which I will call the *alienation view*, holds that anorexia is something external to the person's true self. On this view, the illness is an alien force that overrides, distorts, or masks the person's authentic values and desires. This picture is familiar from clinical practice, including therapeutic techniques that encourage patients to externalise the disorder, to name it, and to treat it as an adversary. It is also attractive in ethical contexts, since it seems to license intervention against a patient's expressed wishes in the name of respecting her real self. The second answer, the *constitution view*, takes patients' reports at face value and holds that anorexia can become genuinely partly constitutive of a person's identity. Proponents of this view point out that the alienation view risks dismissing patients' own self-understanding and imposing a contestable conception of who they "really" are. They also note that it sits uneasily with the long duration of many cases, which often begin in early adolescence, before a stable adult identity has formed.

In this paper I argue that neither view is satisfactory as it stands, and that both rest on an overly simple conception of self-identity. The alienation view presupposes a pre-existing, illness-free self against which the disorder can be measured. The constitution view correctly rejects that presupposition, but it struggles to explain why anorexic identity so often feels unstable, conflicted, and coercive even to those who endorse it. I propose instead that self-identity in anorexia nervosa is best understood as a matter of degree and of dynamic negotiation. It is shaped by the person's evaluative commitments, her embodied self-experience, and the narratives she and others construct about her life. On this account, anorexia can be integrated into a person's identity in ways that are real but partial. The disorder can become part of who someone is while also undermining the conditions under which she could reflectively affirm or revise that identity.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the empirical and phenomenological evidence concerning patients' experience of anorexia as part of the self, and it draws on first-person reports and qualitative research. Section 3 sets out the alienation and constitution views in more detail and identifies the commitments each makes about personal identity and authenticity. Section 4 develops the objections sketched above. In Section 5, I present my alternative account, drawing on narrative and embodied approaches to the self as well as recent work treating anorexia as a kind of passion (Charland et al. 2013). Section 6 considers the implications of this account for debates about capacity, compulsory treatment, and the goals of recovery. I argue that recovery should be understood not as the restoration of a lost self but as the reconstruction of a self capable of genuine self-determination.
